transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-09 16:00 UTC | Duration: ~52m
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Maya Patel (Graybridge Lead Eng), Tom Alvarez (Graybridge CTO), Sarah Kim (Product), Jorge Ruiz (DevOps)
Recording: Host recorded

Summary:
- Intro/demo of Redwood Hosted API for chat/text generation: streaming behavior, key params (temperature, max_tokens, top_p, stop), and retry/idempotency strategy.
- Walked through Console and Optimize suggestions (batching, caching, quantization recommendations) and how to interpret token cost/latency breakdown.
- Agreed to run a short latency benchmark with customer prompts and to share SOC2/security docs.

Topics covered:
- Streaming semantics and partial outputs vs finalization
- Parameterization: temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop sequences, presence/penalty tuning
- Retries: idempotency keys, backoff, resume semantics for streams
- Console: per-route dashboards, token breakdown and per-token cost visualization
- Optimize: batching suggestions and caching KV/prefix reuse
- Security: data residency, SOC 2, encryption/KMS and VPC/dedicated options

Action wrap (short): send docs, run benchmark, schedule follow-up.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Alex Chen: hey everyone thanks for joining, um gonna kick off, uh, quick intros. I'm Alex, I'm the AE on this account, with Priya from infra and runtime.
[00:12] Priya Nair: hey all, hi hi, I'm Priya, I'm an SE, i'll show the runtime behavior and run a quick demo in the console.
[00:18] Maya Patel: Maya here, lead eng for Graybridge, thanks. We are evaluating options for customer-facing chat assistants across our sports and finance verticals. main things: latency and cost.
[00:28] Tom Alvarez: and security; we need SOC2 plus VPC/networking options, potentially on-prem later.
[00:34] Alex Chen: totally understood, we'll touch on hosted first and then point out Dedicated/Private variants for isolation.
[01:05] Priya Nair: ok, demo time — I'm in the Redwood Console, route set to convo-staging, streaming enabled. I'll trigger a sample prompt ("summarize latest earnings call in 3 bullets") so you can see the streaming chunks.
[01:22] (console -> stream begins)
[01:24] Priya Nair: you'll notice partial tokens come in as events, each event is a partial delta; we flush every ~200ms under light load, but the runtime adapts batching windows based on qps and the configured latency SLO.
[01:38] Sarah Kim: can you pause on that — what controls the flush latency? is it tunable?
[01:42] Priya Nair: good question. There are two levers: client-side websocket flush vs runtime batching horizon. the runtime has a target latency SLO per route, and we tune micro-batching to meet that. on Console you can set expected latency and cost preferences — Optimize will suggest batch sizes/quantization.
[02:03] Tom Alvarez: does that mean throughput can change latency unpredictably? we care about p95.
[02:09] Priya Nair: runtime routes by policy; for hosted we have autoscaling and per-tenant isolation to keep p95 stable. for absolute predictability you can use Dedicated (reserved GPU pool). but hosted is usually ok for sub-200ms token times depending on model.
[02:25] Maya Patel: what's the typical token latency for the models you host? numbers pls.
[02:30] Priya Nair: so for a 16k context open model on an A100-like config you'll see single-token latencies in the ~30-80ms range depending on seq length and KV cache hits; cold-start and IO-bound model load can add a few hundred ms. again, Dedicated gives warmer caches.
[03:05] (background noise, someone typing)
[03:18] Alex Chen: quick interjection — we can run a small benchmark with your prompt set to show concrete p50/p95 and token cost, that's probably the clearest path.
[03:25] Maya Patel: yes please. we have some long chats with ~2k tokens average.
[03:30] Priya Nair: note on cost — tokens are the billing unit; Optimize will recommend quantization and batching that can reduce token compute cost without changing semantics too much for chat prompts.
[03:44] Tom Alvarez: about retries — if a stream disconnects mid-response, do you return partial output or is there a way to resume?
[03:51] Priya Nair: great question. hosted streaming is stateless per-request: if the connection drops client-side you'll typically re-issue the request. to avoid duplicate side-effects we recommend using idempotency keys for non-read operations. for streams you can do partial-ack / checkpointing at app layer — we expose a resume token in some SDKs but generally we suggest designing idempotent handlers.
[04:17] Sarah Kim: so resume token is SDK-specific? like ephemeral?
[04:20] Priya Nair: correct, it's SDK that can buffer the last stable token, but it's not a perfect byte-for-byte resume. many customers either replay or build app-level dedupe.
[04:33] (speaker label mismatch) Speaker 3: is there a maximum reconnect window?
[04:36] Priya Nair: we recommend within 30s for user-facing flows; beyond that you should reissue with idempotency semantics.
[04:50] Alex Chen: i'll add that to the runbook we share.
[05:12] Priya Nair: now parameter tuning — temperature. lower = deterministic, higher = creative. top_p is nucleus sampling. here's a quick matrix: for summarization we use temp=0-0.2, top_p=0.8-1.0; for exploratory creative suggestions we go temp=0.8. max_tokens obviously caps cost.
[05:42] Maya Patel: we saw hallucinations with temp at 0.7 on our pipelines; is there a guardrail?
[05:47] Priya Nair: yep, combine lower temperature with stronger system prompt constraints and stop sequences; you can also run a reranker or a short eval model that verifies factualness. Optimize can surface model variants with lower hallucination profiles and recommend regen thresholds.
[06:12] Tom Alvarez: what about stop sequences? any weird tokenization issues?
[06:15] Priya Nair: stop sequences are matched after decode; they can be multi-token and occasionally you might see off-by-1 behavior if model splits tokens differently — test with your exact stop strings.
[06:40] (short pause)
[06:48] Priya Nair: retry strategy: for 5xx and transient network errors do exponential backoff with jitter and idempotency keys for non-idempotent calls. for streaming partials, clients should treat streaming disconnects like a failure and re-request; if you need exactly-once semantics, route through a server-side orchestration that checkpoints.
[07:12] Sarah Kim: can you show a quick code snippet for idempotency in the SDK?
[07:16] Priya Nair: sure, here's a simplified flow, um — generate an idempotency key per user-turn, attach to request header, store local mapping of request->response check, if you get a timeout re-issue with same key. the server will dedupe non-creating calls.
[07:40] (Priya pastes a small snippet, some garbled characters in transcript)
[08:05] Maya Patel: what's the concurrency limit per API key for hosted?
[08:10] Alex Chen: default soft limits are 60 concurrent requests per account, but we can raise for pilots; Dedicated gives predictable throughput.
[08:18] Tom Alvarez: how about per-route throttles?
[08:21] Priya Nair: Console supports per-route quotas and rate-limits; you can put higher priority on critical flows.
[08:36] Jorge Ruiz: for security, we need SSO + SCIM integration and audit logs. also encryption keys on our side.
[08:44] Alex Chen: yes — SSO/SAML, SCIM provisioning, audit logs are supported; for encryption you can use Redwood-managed keys or bring-your-own KMS for Private/Dedicated. SOC2 Type II package is in the security folder I'll share.
[09:00] Sarah Kim: is there an option for data residency? EU data only?
[09:04] Priya Nair: we have region controls; for strict residency we recommend Private with the control plane in your VPC or Dedicated with region pinning.
[09:22] Tom Alvarez: show me Console cost breakdown — where do we see token cost per route?
[09:27] Priya Nair: heading to Console -> Billing -> Routes. here you get token counts, avg tokens per call, and unit cost breakdown by model + quantization profile. there's a graph for cost over time and a table for top routes.
[09:52] (Priya shares a link: https://redwood.example/deck/gb-demo — note: link placeholder)
[10:01] Priya Nair: Optimize suggestions — here's an example: for your stream-heavy route it suggests prefix caching (re-use KV cache on repeated system instructions), switch to int8 quantization for cheaper throughput if quality is acceptable, and a batch policy that groups short requests to improve GPU utilization.
[10:30] Maya Patel: can caching change semantic correctness? if we cache prefixes won't it reuse old context?
[10:36] Priya Nair: caching is safe when prefixes are identical (system prompts, instructions). for user-specific context we don't cache. Optimize flags risky caches and simulates risk.
[10:52] Tom Alvarez: pilot sizing — we want to run a 2-week pilot, ~2k avg tokens, avg qps 5 during spikes to 20. can we get cost estimate?
[11:00] Alex Chen: we'll run a bench with your prompt set and deliver p50/p95 and cost projection.
[11:07] (longer demo continues, Priya toggles streaming and non-streaming modes)
[22:35] Priya Nair: switching to non-streamed (sync) mode shows full payload returned; for low-latency UIs streaming is better because you can render partials and reduce time-to-first-token. but streaming requires client handling of partial updates.
[22:52] Sarah Kim: any browser SDK gotchas?
[22:56] Priya Nair: browsers need websockets or SSE, we provide lightweight wrappers. also watch out for CORS and token expiry; we recommend ephemeral session tokens from your backend.
[23:12] Maya Patel: one more security question — audit logs retention? we need 12 months for compliance.
[23:18] Alex Chen: default 90 days, enterprise add-on for 12+ months; we'll include that in the pricing.
[23:35] Tom Alvarez: do you have a checklist for procurement/legal?
[23:39] Alex Chen: yes i'll attach our procurement checklist and sample MSA.
[23:46] Jorge Ruiz: for Dedicated I assume we can put in our VPC and manage keys?
[23:50] Priya Nair: yes Private and Dedicated both support VPC peering/private endpoints and BYOK via KMS/HSM.
[24:10] (brief silence)
[24:22] Alex Chen: ok to close the loop — next steps: run bench, share SOC2/security docs, and schedule follow-up.
[24:30] Maya Patel: ok sounds good. timeline: we want pilot by Nov 23.
[24:35] Alex Chen: that's reasonable — we'll aim to deliver bench by Nov 16 so you have a week to review.
[24:40] Sarah Kim: any sample prompts we should send? we'll send top 50 user prompts and traffic profile.
[24:46] Maya Patel: will do.
[25:00] (wrap, light chatter)
[25:15] Alex Chen: thanks everyone. Priya, anything to add?
[25:18] Priya Nair: i'll follow up with a short doc on streaming resume patterns and a test harness for the benchmark.
[25:25] Tom Alvarez: thanks.
[25:30] (call ends — remainder is short sideconversations and wrap)
